A tarot deck has 78 cards in two parts.
The 22 Major Arcana, or trumps, are numbered from 0, The Fool, to 21, The World. They stand for the larger themes in a life: beginnings and endings, choices, losses, change, and coming to rest.
The 56 Minor Arcana are four suits of fourteen cards, much like playing cards: ace to ten, and four court cards. They speak of the everyday: work, people, worries, small joys.
A reading puts cards in places that each ask something, and lets the pictures suggest an answer. The cards describe; they do not decide anything, and they do not tell the future.
Cups are feeling: love, friendship, the heart and what it wants.
Swords are thought: decisions, words, conflict and truth, and the worry a busy mind makes.
Wands are drive and will: energy, ambition, the start of things and the push to see them through.
Pentacles are the material and practical: work, money, the body, home and the slow building of things.

The numbers run roughly from a seed to a harvest. An ace is the suit at its first and purest; the middle numbers are its tests and turns; a ten is the suit carried as far as it goes, for better or worse.

The court cards are often read as people, or as ways of being. A page is a student or a message; a knight is the suit in motion, sometimes too fast; a queen holds the suit from the inside; a king holds it outwardly, with authority.
A card can come out upside down. A reversed card usually suggests the card’s meaning blocked, delayed, turned inward, or taken too far, rather than simply its opposite.
Each card here has an upright and a reversed meaning, and its page shows both, with the one that applies to how it was drawn first.
Some readers do not use reversals at all. Switch them off in Settings, under Reversed cards, and every card comes out upright, the card for today included.
Before a reading, hold a question in mind. An open question works better than a yes or no one: “What should I know about…” rather than “Will…”. No question at all is fine too.
One card: a single card for the question, or for the day. Simple, and often enough.
Past, present, future: three cards, left to right. What led here, where things stand, and where they seem to be going if nothing changes.

Celtic Cross: ten cards, from Waite. In the cross: 1, the heart of the matter; 2, laid across it, what helps or hinders; 3, above, what is aimed at or hoped for; 4, beneath, the ground it stands on; 5, what is passing; 6, what is coming.
Up the staff on the right: 7, you, and how you meet it; 8, the people and place around you; 9, hopes and fears, which are often the same thing; 10, where it leads.
Read each card in its place, then look at the spread as a whole: which suits gather, how many trumps there are, which way the figures face.
The pictures are Pamela Colman Smith’s, drawn for the deck Arthur Edward Waite devised and Rider published in London in 1909.

They come from scans of an original 1909 “Roses & Lilies” printing, made by Saskia Jansen from her own deck and published on Wikimedia Commons. The drawings are in the public domain. Here they are in sixteen greys, for this screen.
The meanings are written for this app in plain words, drawing on Waite’s The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), which is also in the public domain.
A daily card, spreads and a journal of readings, with the 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith deck.

Everything you put in this app stays on this phone. It has no internet access, so nothing is sent anywhere, and nothing is collected about you. There are no ads, no analytics and no tracking. Backups and exports go only where you choose to save them. The two addresses below open in your browser only when you press them.
